questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Most crucial of all for me was the ranking of the university. I chose the University of Amsterdam because of its well-renowned Anthropology faculty. Because of its high ranking, it opens up more opportunities for me with regards to where i want to take my Master's degree.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: In terms of social aspects, i had an incredible experience. The university provided a much more multicultural student environment, and a lot more engaging teaching methods, as students were typically expected to take over the class for at least one of the modules. The student accommodation was great. Although quite expensive (around 600 Euros per month), it didn't bother me too much, as the quality was good - plus the price would be similar in Copenhagen anyway. A significant drawback for me, however, was the fact that one of my lecturers had to go on sick leave in the middle of a course - which is fair enough of course. But the university left us in the dark for around 2 months, with no updates regarding the course, although they expressed that we would be allowed to finish it anyway. After these 2 months, the course was taken up by 4 different lecturers who - albeit understandably - lacked knowledge of the curriculum. More transparency from the university's administration, and more communication between the different teachers would've been appreciated.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Incredibly easy. A lot of practical information was provided by our landlords (DeKey), and the student help-desks at the university helped me a lot. My fellow students in my accommodation were also quick to let people know about practical matters.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We were given a tour of the university, taking us through the different departments, showing us where to get coffee or how to work the printers. We had several zoom meetings with general information in the beginning as well. I knew most of this just from reading the university's website, which is quite easy to navigate as well.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: We were living just outside of the Roeterseiland campus in the Plantage area. These spots were highly sought-after, so i only got them as i was ready to pounce just as the housing application website went live. You could get your own room or share a 2 bedroom 'apartment' with someone else. People typically lived with 5-8 people on their floor. Many of the late applicants ended up in a highrise building south of the city, which was a bit of a struggle for them as far as i heard - Having a 30 minute bike-ride to university.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: We had our own kitchen. We didn't coordinate any meal plans as such, but cooked together at times. We had three fridges - a bit excessive for 5 people - two micro-wave ovens, an electric stove, a boiler, dish-washing machine, etc. We had everything we needed except a normal oven.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Make sure to lock your doors. We had issues with the front door and one night a stranger did try to get into our floor. There were stories of some students stealing from each other as well, although i cannot vouch for their authenticity. Be sure to mind your neighbours as well - the landlord was quick to let us know, but many students got caught up in a 'touristy' mentality, wanting to throw house-parties until the early morning, etc. We did get several complaints throughout our stay.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was all done online prior to my stay. You have to be quick to get it sorted, because if you're not registered, you won't be able to apply for housing through the university - which makes things a lot easier in terms of finding accommodation. You had to upload a passport photo, transcript of records, general info about your studies, etc.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There were several help-desks you could call or write e-mails to. And the website was very helpful as well.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Although i logged in immediately once registration opened, most of the classes i wanted was taken. However, there was still many interesting things to register for. I put myself on the waiting list for some courses, which soon opened up as it seemed people had 'over-registrated' (picked several more courses than allowed). I ended up with some really interesting courses despite all of this.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be quick. Have an online atomic clock ready in another window, so you can click on the link the second it opens. I was 6 seconds late, and far behind in the queue. Although i presume many are already familiar with this sort of thing from buying concert or festival tickets online.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Some were very challenging. Especially as i haven't written academically in English before. One course was especially difficult, which made sense, as it was for third-years only and 12 ECTS instead of the usual 6 for elective courses. The university values critical thinking and active engagement, so the expectations of the student participation in classes are much higher than in Copenhagen. However, I enjoyed this very much, and i learnt a lot, both within and outside the classroom during my stay.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was a lot more engaging. At times the student-teacher hierarchy dissipated completely, especially during presentations, because students were expected to facilitate discussions afterwards, which often involved the teacher in a 'student' role. This created a much more equitable class environment.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Brazil: Democracy, Citizenship, and Culture
Political Anthropology: The Norm, Violence, and Resistance
Anthropology of the Middle East
Education & International Development

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend all of the above to be honest.
Political Anthropology has one of the most interesting curriculums i've ever come across. It teaches students how to engage politically with their field of study, and to not be afraid of taking a stance as an anthropologist. The freedom to choose your own subject for the final essay was great aswell. It challenged me to be more independent in my research process. 
Anthropology of the Middle East is a short course, that doesn't do justice to the scope of study it encapsulates. However, i would recommend this to everyone who has been subjected to the narrative of a 'War on Terror'. An eye-opening course, which invites the student to critically reflect on their Western gaze, without portraying cultural difference as something insurmountable. 
The Brazil course was especially interesting due to its political relevancy, and we engaged with Bolsonaro quite a bit throughout the course. However, there was also plenty of time to focus on the indigenous peoples of Brazil, and the teaching-team was perfectly composed to facilitate both of these perspectives. 
Educaton & International Development was the shortest course i took (lasting 3-4 weeks), however, it was very interesting as it introduces students to alternative pedagogies and draws them in as co-creators of the course. The empirical subject changes every year, so the course remains ever-relevant as well.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I spent a lot of money on food delivery during the exam periods. In terms of the nightlife of Amsterdam it's very expensive as well. Not just the drinks, but the tickets - it seemed the whole city was on a ticketing system at times. Price ranges vary a lot, so you can find some on the cheap - they ranged from 5 to 40 Euros in my experience.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Transport is very, very cheap if you get a bike. You can also rent one quite cheaply through Swapfiets. A bike will get you anywhere in town in 40 minutes tops, and the infrastructure is suprisingly superior to Copenhagen in terms of cycling. You are much safer as a cyclist, as there is always some form of barriers protecting you from traffic. It is also much better designed for long-distance cycling, as you never really have to stop at a red light.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Amazing nightlife. Perfect for a mental detox in terms of the Corona-period.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: We had a student bar - CREA - with cheap prices. The building was also used for band practice, dance lessons, theater, etc. And i believe it is quite easy to sign up.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: They have the largest flea market in Europe up in Amsterdam Noord every saturday. Many interesting artists are exhibited in the city's museums (Hieronymus Bosch recommended). Rokin Subway Station has an exhibition of all the things they dug up during its construction lined up in a huge glass box along its escalators. The city has many parks with excellent facilities for recreational sports.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: See above.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Extremely easy. Locals oftentimes told me that Amsterdam is not really the Netherlands, in the sense that everyone speaks English, and is from outside the country. The place is so multicultural that you can never really feel out of place - at least i never did. Besides, being from Copenhagen it's easy to adjust to the mode of transportation - cycling - and the prices - seemingly extortionary just like home.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Leave your own culture behind. Don't try to impose your own values on others. Don't expect everything to work as intended. Don't be too nice - it can come across as boring. In terms of the Dutch locals, they are somewhat more reserved, and therefore harder to get to know, but we are used to that back home i guess.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Language - I found Dutch discernible when reading, but absolutely alien when they were speaking. 
A very phlegmy language.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The vibrancy, outspokenness, visual aesthetics, and the fact that it was never really singular but multifaceted as a culture.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Again, don't be too nice, don't be afraid to step outside of your comfort zone, and be sure to structure your time to meet the deadlines - at the end of the day, you're there to study, and if you engage with your responsibilities as a student you will have a very fruitful learning experience.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be careful not to get sucked into 'monocultural social groups'. There were two huge social groups of English and Latin American students respectively, who very rarely engaged with people outside of their groups. I got to know people from both sections, and although they were more comfortable in the beginning, i felt sorry for them in the end - as they seemed to miss out on the most vital part of exchange for me--engaging with other cultures.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The social life - i met people from all over - From Japan to South Africa, Canada, Australia, Argentina - even someone from Monaco and Luxembourg.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Structuring the time and meeting deadlines.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
